store.0: I have been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it has been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It has given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's fascinating to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't initially see myself going down the research route. I was into coding projects and hackathons, but I didn't consider research as something that aligned with my interests. However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She informed me about an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant due to the intimidation factor, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.
store.1: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists collaborate with experts from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work together to make massive datasets more comprehensible. In contrast to the small datasets we typically handle in classes, our datasets are tens of terabytes in size. My main task involves creating front-end prototypes that present data slices in dynamic, interactive dashboards. To achieve this, I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.
store.2: The first research project I really got into involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific, with each day's data stored in separate files on different servers. Our task was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent manner, showing patterns over months or years. I took on the challenge head-on, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designing interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. Eventually, I co-authored a paper on this system. Seeing my name in an official publication was surreal and one of my proudest moments in college.
store.3: My current research has shifted towards immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' understanding of complex data. It's a leap from traditional data visualization methods like spreadsheets and 2D graphs. By allowing scientists to interact with 3D representations in a virtual environment, we can provide a more intuitive experience. This field is still in its early stages, and there's a lot of experimentation involved, such as integrating VR headsets, engines like Unity or Unreal, and optimizing data streaming into 3D environments. It's exciting to be at the forefront of this cutting-edge field, where every day brings new challenges and opportunities to forge our own path.
store.4: Research life is often misunderstood as me sitting in a quiet corner coding away on a mysterious project. However, it's actually a lot of reading. Academic papers never end, and when I'm trying to solve a bug with rendering volumetric data in VR, there's a good chance someone has attempted something similar and written about it in a conference proceeding or workshop. I need to comb through these papers to find relevant information. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively, focusing on the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine if a paper is relevant before diving into the details. Occasionally, when I discover something interesting, I share it with the rest of the lab, and we discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
store.5: I have the opportunity to interact with a diverse group of graduate students, including master's and PhD candidates. Initially, it can be intimidating to collaborate with individuals who are deeply immersed in their niche fields. However, it's also incredibly inspiring. One PhD student in our lab is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He's working to integrate this algorithm with our VR platform, aiming to reduce the need for loading every single data point at once. This approach can significantly enhance real-time performance when dealing with massive datasets like climate data. Working alongside him allows me to witness the practical application of advanced theoretical concepts. Some of our most productive brainstorming sessions occur spontaneously, often during casual conversations in the lab break room or over coffee. We discuss strategies for offloading processing tasks to the GPU, which can greatly improve performance.
store.6: I have had the opportunity to participate in a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience, as it forced me to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous, worrying about professors or industry professionals asking tough questions. However, the reality was quite different. People were genuinely interested in what I was doing, and it turned out to be more of a friendly dialogue. I even met a few folks from local startups who shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to the potential for research to transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.7: I have been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and am currently working on a larger conference submission for the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS). This conference is a significant event in our field. Our paper focuses on a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. We hypothesize that VR immersion enables researchers to identify anomalies or trends more quickly than with a standard 2D chart. To test this, we conducted a small user trial with 15 participants, recording their times and gathering UX questionnaire feedback. Now, we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort, with different team members handling specific sections. I'm responsible for the system architecture and prototype design, while others are working on the user study methodology, and our PI is weaving everything together into a cohesive narrative. It's a delicate balancing act, especially considering my senior coursework and capstone project commitments.
store.8: I have been considering my future plans, and I'm currently leaning towards working in the industry for a couple of years. I hope to find a tech company that values R&D and advanced solution building. This will give me the opportunity to see how cutting-edge concepts like data visualization and machine learning are applied in real product development. One of my mentors suggested that industry experience can provide a better understanding of the problems that are truly relevant, which will make me a more practical researcher if I decide to pursue a PhD in the future. It's a great way to gain both theoretical knowledge and practical experience.
store.9: I have experienced my share of frustration in research, where weeks of work on a particular approach may not yield the desired results, or I discover that someone else has already explored and improved upon the same idea. It can be disheartening, but the key is to adapt and incorporate the existing research into our own work. By reading the existing paper, we can build upon their findings, explore new angles or applications, and push the boundaries further. This is the essence of research – building upon the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special. It's a reminder that we're not starting from scratch, but rather contributing to a larger body of knowledge.
store.10: One memorable experience that stands out was when one of our servers crashed a few months ago. We had vital data stored there, some of which wasn't fully backed up(a rookie mistake, I know). The scramble that night was intense: frantic email chains, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to determine if we could recover the data. Fortunately, we were able to restore most of it, but that crisis highlighted the importance of data backups. Afterward, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we wouldn't rely on a single point of failure again. It was stressful, but it also brought the lab together. We learned a valuable lesson and became more vigilant in our data management.
store.11: Research has allowed me to form meaningful connections with professors beyond the classroom. My PI is incredibly approachable, and I can easily reach out to her for guidance on career direction or help with academic struggles. She has also been instrumental in recommending me for scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I recently attended a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, which brought together experts from around the world. Witnessing them engage in technical discussions, propose new frameworks, and exchange good-natured jabs over rival theories was fascinating. It felt like I was experiencing the cutting-edge of CS knowledge in real time. These experiences have been invaluable in shaping my understanding of the field and expanding my professional network.
store.12: My journey in the research world has been a mix of hard work, chaos, and rewards. It's a feeling that what I do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data in the future. The VR and immersive technologies we're pioneering could become standard tools, and I'd be proud to say I was part of that from the beginning. The sense of contributing to something bigger is what keeps me motivated. Whether or not I pursue a graduate degree soon, this experience has transformed my perspective on computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergraduate years without it – it's enriched my understanding of what it means to be a computer scientist.
